Beach Boys songs.California Dreamin': Trap: this 1965 classic belongs to The Mamas and the Papas, though John Phillips of that group later co-wrote the Beach Boys' Kokomo.
Beach Boys songs.Surfin' Bird: The Trashmen's 1963 novelty hit was stitched together from two Rivingtons songs; the surf-sounding title fooled people, but it isn't by the Beach Boys.
Beach Boys songs.Hotel California: Eagles, 1976. The Beach Boys sing about California a lot, but this long, moody road song belongs to Don Henley and Glenn Frey's band.
Beach Boys songs.Wipe Out: The Surfaris' 1963 instrumental, famous for its drum solo; the cackling intro was supplied by a producer, and it's a surf rival, not the Beach Boys.
Beach Boys songs.Mr. Tambourine Man: Bob Dylan wrote it, but The Byrds' jangly 1965 version hit number one and helped invent folk rock; the Beach Boys never owned it.
Beach Boys songs.Monday Monday: The Mamas and the Papas, 1966. It won a Grammy and sounds sun-soaked, but it's another California band, not Brian Wilson's.
Beach Boys songs.Happy Together: The Turtles, 1967. It famously knocked The Beatles' Penny Lane off the top spot, and a cheerful title doesn't make it a Beach Boys song.
Beach Boys songs.Daydream Believer: A Monkees hit from 1967, written by John Stewart of the Kingston Trio and sung by Davy Jones; nothing to do with the Beach Boys.
Beach Boys songs.Do Wah Diddy: Manfred Mann took it to number one in 1964, from a song first recorded by the Exciters; a British band, not the California one.
Beach Boys songs.Pipeline: The Chantays' 1963 surf instrumental, named for the Hawaiian wave; it fits the beach mood, but it isn't the Beach Boys.
Beach Boys songs.Mrs. Robinson: Simon and Garfunkel wrote it for the film The Graduate; it's folk rock, with no Beach Boys connection, despite the era.
Beach Boys songs.Summer in the City: The Lovin' Spoonful, 1966. Car horns and jackhammer noises mimic a hot New York street, a sound far from Beach Boys surf.
Beach Boys songs.Good Day Sunshine: The Beatles on Revolver, 1966, written by Paul McCartney; the sunny title tempts, but it's not by Brian Wilson's group.

Kinds of guitar.Acoustic guitar: It makes sound with a hollow wooden body, and no amplifier is needed.
Kinds of guitar.Electric guitar: Les Paul and Leo Fender pioneered solid-body models in the early 1950s, and pickups turn string vibration into signal.
Kinds of guitar.Bass guitar: It typically has four strings tuned like a double bass, and Leo Fender's 1951 Precision Bass made it portable.
Kinds of guitar.Classical guitar: Nylon strings give it a warm, mellow sound, and it has a wider neck than a steel-string guitar.
Kinds of guitar.Twelve-string: It has six pairs of strings, with the extra ones tuned an octave higher, giving it a shimmering chime, as heard in "Hotel California".
Kinds of guitar.Steel-string: The standard folk and country acoustic, and its metal strings make a brighter, louder tone than nylon ones.
Kinds of guitar.Resonator guitar: Metal cones in its body made it louder in the 1920s before electric amplification, and it is the signature of bluegrass dobro.
Kinds of guitar.Lap steel guitar: Played flat across the lap with a metal bar, it gives country and Hawaiian music their sliding sound.
Kinds of guitar.Flamenco guitar: It is lighter than a classical guitar and has tap plates, and players rap on the body for rhythm.
Kinds of guitar.Archtop guitar: Its carved arched top and f-holes, like a violin, made it a jazz staple.
Kinds of guitar.Air guitar: There is even an Air Guitar World Championships in Finland, held since 1996, and judges score it on "airness".
Kinds of guitar.Banjo: It is a different instrument, usually with five strings and a drum-like body.
Kinds of guitar.Mandolin: It has eight strings in four pairs, and is tuned like a violin, so it is not a type of guitar.
Kinds of guitar.Sitar: An Indian long-necked instrument with sympathetic strings, and George Harrison helped bring it to rock.
Kinds of guitar.Harp: Its strings are plucked but run perpendicular to its soundboard, and it is not a guitar.
Kinds of guitar.Cello: It is bowed and it is tuned in fifths, and it sits between your knees.
Kinds of guitar.Violin: Violins are bowed rather than plucked, and are tuned in fifths, unlike guitars.
Kinds of guitar.Zither: Its strings are stretched over a flat sound box, and the "Third Man Theme" made it famous in 1949.
Kinds of guitar.Double bass: The tallest string instrument in the orchestra, and it is a bowed cousin of the viol family, not a guitar.
Kinds of guitar.Harpsichord: It has keys that pluck strings, and it is a keyboard instrument.
Kinds of guitar.Dulcimer: The Appalachian version is held on the lap and its name comes from Latin for "sweet", and it is not a guitar.
Kinds of guitar.Keytar: It is a keyboard slung like a guitar, popular in the 1980s, and it does not have strings.
Kinds of guitar.Theremin: It is played without touching it, by moving hands near two antennas, and was invented in Russia in 1920.
Kinds of guitar.Autoharp: It has chord bars that mute certain strings, and the instrument is strummed like a zither, not fretted like a guitar.

Tennis terms.Love: Love for zero may come from the French l'oeuf, the egg, though some say it's from playing for love, meaning for nothing.
Tennis terms.Deuce: At 40-all the game isn't won until someone leads by two points, and the word probably comes from the French à deux.
Tennis terms.Ace: Serves above 250 km/h have been recorded in men's tennis, and an ace is one the receiver cannot touch.
Tennis terms.Advantage: After deuce, the next point gives advantage, and the player needs to win another point to take the game.
Tennis terms.Break point: A break point is a chance to win a game on the opponent's serve, which is why a break is so decisive in a set.
Tennis terms.Volley: A volley is a shot hit before the ball bounces, usually near the net, and it takes much faster reflexes than groundstrokes.
Tennis terms.Lob: A lob sends the ball high over a net player's head, and a well-timed one can win a point against an aggressive opponent at the net.
Tennis terms.Baseline: The baseline is the back line of the court, and players who stay behind it and trade groundstrokes are known as baseliners.
Tennis terms.Tiebreak: A tiebreak decides a set at six games all, and it was introduced in the 1970s to end marathon sets; Wimbledon's 2019 rule added a final-set one.
Tennis terms.Double fault: A double fault loses the point when both serves miss, and it is the server's own mistake rather than the opponent's win.
Tennis terms.Let: A let is a serve that clips the net and lands in the right box, and it's replayed; the word comes from an old English word meaning hinder.
Tennis terms.Birdie: Birdie is one under par in golf and has no meaning in tennis, where a scoring jump is love, 15, 30 and 40.
Tennis terms.Bogey: Bogey in golf means one over par, and tennis has no par to measure against.
Tennis terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's three stumps; Wimbledon's grass courts share only a love of turf with a cricket pitch.
Tennis terms.Touchdown: A touchdown belongs to American football and has no place in tennis, where players are not allowed to carry the ball.
Tennis terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball is a tenpin bowling mistake and in tennis the nearest thing is hitting the net cord.
Tennis terms.Bullseye: A bullseye is the center of a target and is common in darts, whereas tennis aims at the lines.
Tennis terms.Home run: A home run is baseball's fence-clearing hit, and in tennis a ball hit out of the court is simply out.
Tennis terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball, though tennis has its own slam: a Grand Slam means winning all four majors in one year.
Tennis terms.Hat trick: A hat trick is three goals or wickets, a term from cricket, not tennis.
Tennis terms.Scrum: A scrum is a rugby formation, and tennis has no contact whatsoever between the players.
Tennis terms.Icing: Icing is an ice hockey rule on shooting the puck down the rink, not a tennis term.
Tennis terms.Bunt: A bunt is a soft baseball hit with the bat held still, not a tennis term, though the drop shot is the same idea.
Tennis terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess, and tennis ends with the final point instead, so no king is cornered.

Knitting and crochet words.Purl: The purl stitch is the knit stitch's mirror, with the loop going in from the front. Alternating them makes stockinette's smooth fabric.
Knitting and crochet words.Cast on: Every piece of knitting starts by looping a first row of stitches onto the needle. There are dozens of ways, each with different stretch.
Knitting and crochet words.Bind off: Finishing a piece by lifting each stitch over the next locks it in place. Done too tightly, it makes an edge that won't stretch.
Knitting and crochet words.Yarn over: Wrapping the yarn around the needle makes a deliberate hole while adding a stitch. Lace knitters use it to build delicate patterns.
Knitting and crochet words.Skein: A loose oval coil of yarn is a skein. It is the same word for a flock of geese in flight, from an old French term.
Knitting and crochet words.Gauge: Knitters count stitches per inch or per ten centimeters, and skipping this swatch is how sweaters end up two sizes off.
Knitting and crochet words.Stockinette: Knit rows with purl rows alternating produce a smooth front with bumpy back, and the fabric tends to curl at its edges.
Knitting and crochet words.Garter stitch: Knitting every row gives rippled ridges that lie flat with no curling. It's the usual first stitch beginners learn.
Knitting and crochet words.Cable knit: Crossing groups of stitches makes rope-like twists. The style is linked to Irish Aran sweaters, from the Aran Islands.
Knitting and crochet words.Knitting needles: The pair of long pointed sticks has been made of bone, wood, bamboo, steel and carbon fiber, and sizes run by millimeter.
Knitting and crochet words.Crochet hook: Instead of two needles, crochet uses a single hooked tool, and the word crochet comes from the French for hook.
Knitting and crochet words.Ribbing: Alternating knit and purl columns gives a stretchy fabric that hugs the body, so it's what cuffs and sweater hems use.
Knitting and crochet words.Kiln: Potters fire clay in this oven, which can reach well over 1,000 degrees Celsius. It's got nothing to do with yarn.
Knitting and crochet words.Glaze: A ceramic coating of ground glass-forming minerals melts in the kiln into a glassy skin. It has no connection to yarn crafts.
Knitting and crochet words.Easel: The word comes from Dutch for donkey, as the frame carries a painting's load. It belongs to painters.
Knitting and crochet words.Gesso: This chalky white primer prepares canvas or wood panels for painting. The name is Italian for chalk, and it's no yarn craft.
Knitting and crochet words.Tripod: A camera's three-legged support keeps long exposures sharp, and it belongs in a photographer's bag rather than a knitter's.
Knitting and crochet words.Aperture: The lens opening that controls how much light reaches the sensor is a photography term, not a yarn one.
Knitting and crochet words.Shutter: A camera's shutter opens briefly to expose the sensor, and speeds can be as brief as a few thousandths of a second.
Knitting and crochet words.Chisel: This edged hand tool is for carving wood or stone, and it has more in common with a sculptor's kit than yarn.
Knitting and crochet words.Dovetail: Interlocking fan-shaped pins and tails make a woodworking joint strong enough that drawers have held together for centuries.
Knitting and crochet words.Soldering iron: Electronics workers use this hot tool to melt metal joins, at roughly 300 degrees Celsius. It's not a stitching tool.
Knitting and crochet words.Fret saw: This thin-bladed saw cuts tight curves in thin wood, and it's what scroll-work makers use, not yarn crafters.
Knitting and crochet words.Lathe: A machine that spins wood or metal against a cutting tool. Lathes are among the oldest machine tools, with roots in ancient Egypt.

Pottery and ceramics words.Kiln: Firing in this oven turns soft clay into permanent ceramic, and temperatures can top 1,200 degrees Celsius for stoneware.
Pottery and ceramics words.Glaze: Ground minerals suspended in water are brushed on, then melt in the kiln into a glassy skin. Raw glazes often look dull and chalky.
Pottery and ceramics words.Clay: Fine particles of weathered rock give it its plasticity, and clay is shaped wet but turned to stone-hard ceramic by fire.
Pottery and ceramics words.Potter's wheel: Spinning wheels for pots appeared in Mesopotamia over 5,000 years ago, and they let potters make round forms far faster than by hand.
Pottery and ceramics words.Slip: Clay thinned with water to a creamy liquid acts as decoration or as glue for joining pieces, such as attaching a handle to a mug.
Pottery and ceramics words.Bisque: The first firing, usually at a lower heat, hardens the clay into porous ware ready to absorb glaze. The word isn't connected to the soup.
Pottery and ceramics words.Greenware: Unfired clay, dried but not yet fired, is fragile and called by this name, though it isn't green at all.
Pottery and ceramics words.Wedging: Potters knead clay like bread dough to remove air bubbles, since a trapped bubble can explode in the kiln and wreck neighboring pots.
Pottery and ceramics words.Raku: This Japanese firing style pulls pots red-hot from the kiln and puts them into combustibles, producing crackled glazes and smoky blacks.
Pottery and ceramics words.Stoneware: Fired at high temperatures, it becomes dense and waterproof without glaze, which is why it's a favorite for everyday dishes.
Pottery and ceramics words.Porcelain: Chinese potters perfected it by about the 7th to 10th century, and Europe didn't reproduce it until about 1708 in Meissen.
Pottery and ceramics words.Earthenware: Low-fired and porous, it's the oldest sort of pottery, and unglazed pots like terracotta flowerpots leak moisture.
Pottery and ceramics words.Easel: A stand for painters' canvases, so it's not clay-related. Its name comes from the Dutch word for donkey.
Pottery and ceramics words.Gesso: Painters coat canvases with this chalk-based primer. The word is Italian for chalk.
Pottery and ceramics words.Purl: This is a knitting stitch, the reverse of knit, and it belongs to yarn work, not clay.
Pottery and ceramics words.Skein: A loose coil of yarn, and also a flock of geese in flight. Not a pottery term.
Pottery and ceramics words.Aperture: A lens opening, which controls how much light a camera takes in, so it belongs to photography.
Pottery and ceramics words.Bokeh: A photographer's term from Japanese for blur, describing how a lens renders out-of-focus areas.
Pottery and ceramics words.Bobbin: The small spool that holds thread in a sewing machine, so it belongs to sewing rather than the potter's studio.
Pottery and ceramics words.Thimble: A sewer's finger shield, not a studio tool. Some are made of porcelain, though, as collectors' keepsakes.
Pottery and ceramics words.Router: A spinning-bit woodworking power tool for grooves and edges, though in networking the word means something else.
Pottery and ceramics words.Crochet hook: The single hooked tool of crochet, and unrelated to clay, whose potters use ribs and needle tools instead.
Pottery and ceramics words.Tripod: A camera stand with three legs, so it belongs to photographers, though pottery has tripod stilts that hold wares apart in kilns.
Pottery and ceramics words.Hand plane: A woodworker's smoothing tool, so it shaves wood, not clay.

Things a sore loser might do.Flip the board: In Japan, flipping the table in rage is such a trope it has a name: chabudai gaeshi.
Things a sore loser might do.Sulk: Losses sting roughly twice as much as equal wins please, a bias psychologists call loss aversion.
Things a sore loser might do.Demand a rematch: Not always petty: Garry Kasparov demanded a rematch after losing to Deep Blue in 1997, but IBM declined.
Things a sore loser might do.Blame the ref: An old excuse, though sometimes fair: Frank Lampard's disallowed goal at the 2010 World Cup pushed FIFA toward goal-line technology.
Things a sore loser might do.Storm off: Walking away mid-game is a classic tantrum, and in tournament rules it usually counts as a forfeit.
Things a sore loser might do.Accuse of cheating: In 2022 Magnus Carlsen's suspicion of Hans Niemann shook the chess world and led to a lawsuit.
Things a sore loser might do.Throw the controller: Nintendo added wrist straps to Wii remotes after players hurled them through TVs.
Things a sore loser might do.Pout: A pout is an old human signal: it shows displeasure without words, and often seeks sympathy.
Things a sore loser might do.Quit mid-game: Online games punish leavers with penalties or matchmaking bans, because one quitter can ruin a match for everyone.
Things a sore loser might do.Rage quit: Gamer slang that spread with online multiplayer in the 2000s, for exiting a game in a fury.
Things a sore loser might do.Whine: Aesop's fox who called the grapes sour after failing to reach them is the oldest sore loser in fiction.
Things a sore loser might do.Smash a racket: Alexander Zverev was disqualified in Acapulco in 2024 for hitting the umpire's chair with his racket.
Things a sore loser might do.Shake hands: NHL teams line up for a handshake after every playoff series, even bitter rivals, in a famed tradition.
Things a sore loser might do.Say good game: GG, good game, is a standard esports courtesy, though it is sometimes typed sarcastically.
Things a sore loser might do.Congratulate: Many leagues formalise it, with beaten teams applauding the champions in a guard of honour.
Things a sore loser might do.Smile: A genuine smile uses the muscles around the eyes, known as a Duchenne smile, which helps a graceful loser look sincere.
Things a sore loser might do.Clap: Polite applause for a winner is expected in golf and tennis, where crowds stay quiet during play.
Things a sore loser might do.Hug opponent: Jesse Owens and German rival Luz Long became friends in Berlin in 1936 after Long gave Owens advice.
Things a sore loser might do.Thank the ref: Rugby players routinely thank the referee, whose word is final and who is addressed as sir.
Things a sore loser might do.Laugh it off: Humour is linked to coping with stress, so laughing off a loss helps players move on.
Things a sore loser might do.Help clean up: At the 2018 World Cup, Japanese fans tidied their stands after matches, and the team left its dressing room spotless.
Things a sore loser might do.Bow: In judo, kendo and sumo a bow shows respect for opponent and place before and after bouts.
Things a sore loser might do.High five: Often credited to the Dodgers' Glenn Burke and Dusty Baker in 1977.
Things a sore loser might do.Cheer for the winner: Cheering for the one who beat you is the sign of a gracious loser, so it's the opposite of sore.

Games where something or someone hides.Hide and seek: Counting before searching is the standard opening. In Japan it's kakurenbo, and similar games are very ancient.
Games where something or someone hides.Sardines: Hide and seek in reverse: one person hides, and each finder squeezes in beside them. The last seeker loses.
Games where something or someone hides.Kick the can: Combines tag and hide and seek: hiders can be freed by someone kicking the can before they are caught.
Games where something or someone hides.Hide the thimble: A Victorian parlour game: players hunt a thimble in plain sight, guided by hot and cold hints.
Games where something or someone hides.Geocaching: A GPS treasure hunt that began in May 2000, after the US stopped deliberately scrambling civilian GPS signals.
Games where something or someone hides.Easter egg hunt: Children search for hidden eggs. The White House Easter Egg Roll has been held since 1878.
Games where something or someone hides.Hot and cold: Seekers get hints of warmer or colder as they near the hidden object.
Games where something or someone hides.Manhunt: A team version of tag and hide and seek, usually played after dark with flashlights.
Games where something or someone hides.Treasure hunt: Pirates rarely buried treasure. The popular image owes much to Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island, published in 1883.
Games where something or someone hides.Tag: A chase game with nothing to hide, since everyone is visible all along.
Games where something or someone hides.Leapfrog: Players vault over crouched partners. Shakespeare's Henry V has the earliest known use of the word.
Games where something or someone hides.Hopscotch: Roman children drew hopscotch courts about 2,000 years ago, but nothing is hidden.
Games where something or someone hides.Duck Duck Goose: A circle chase game. In Minnesota it's called Duck, Duck, Grey Duck.
Games where something or someone hides.Simon Says: You obey commands only if they start with Simon says. It tests listening, not searching.
Games where something or someone hides.Musical chairs: Players race to a seat when music stops, with one fewer chair each round.
Games where something or someone hides.Tug of war: It was an Olympic event from 1900 to 1920, and Britain won the last gold.
Games where something or someone hides.Red Rover: Two lines try to break through linked arms. Many schools have banned it for injuries.
Games where something or someone hides.Four square: Players bounce a ball between four squares. Nothing is hidden.
Games where something or someone hides.Jump rope: Dutch settlers brought double Dutch to America. Nothing is hidden.
Games where something or someone hides.Dodgeball: Foam balls are thrown at players, and it even has a World Dodgeball Federation.
Games where something or someone hides.Charades: It began as a French verse riddle in the 18th century, then became silent acting.
Games where something or someone hides.Twister: Hands and feet go on coloured circles on a mat. Everything is in plain view.
Games where something or someone hides.Limbo: Limbo began in Trinidad as a funeral wake dance, and nothing hides.
Games where something or someone hides.Marbles: Players flick marbles to knock others from a ring.

Jobs at a sports match.Referee: The referee enforces the laws of the game and can issue penalties. In football, the whistle and cards are his main tools.
Jobs at a sports match.Umpire: In cricket, tennis and baseball, umpires rule on play. Cricket's third umpire uses video replay.
Jobs at a sports match.Linesman: Now called assistant referees in football, linesmen use flags to signal offside, throw-ins and corners.
Jobs at a sports match.Ball boy: Ball boys and girls retrieve balls, and at Wimbledon they are trained through intense auditions.
Jobs at a sports match.Caddie: Caddies carry a golfer's clubs and give advice. The word is probably from the French 'cadet', for a younger son.
Jobs at a sports match.Coach: The word 'coach' once meant a carriage, and slang at Oxford turned it into a tutor, later extended to sport.
Jobs at a sports match.Commentator: Commentators describe live action for broadcast, and the best become as famous as the players.
Jobs at a sports match.Groundskeeper: A groundskeeper prepares the playing surface, and at Wimbledon, grass is cut to exactly 8 millimeters.
Jobs at a sports match.Mascot: Mascots entertain fans in costume. The word comes from French for lucky charm.
Jobs at a sports match.Scorekeeper: The scorekeeper records points, and in baseball, the scorebook has complex notation that fans can read like a story of the game.
Jobs at a sports match.Timekeeper: Timekeepers track official game time, and in boxing, they ring the bell for rounds.
Jobs at a sports match.Physio: A physio treats injuries on the touchline, and their rapid response can decide whether a player continues.
Jobs at a sports match.Dentist: A dentist works in a clinic, though some pro sports teams employ dental staff, and mouthguards often come from them.
Jobs at a sports match.Pilot: Pilots fly planes. At a match, pilots only show up in flypasts, not as part of the game staff.
Jobs at a sports match.Librarian: A librarian works in a library, with no role at a game.
Jobs at a sports match.Barista: Baristas make coffee in cafes. A match may have a concession seller, but that's another job.
Jobs at a sports match.Plumber: Plumbers fix pipes. Not usually seen at match day, except behind the scenes.
Jobs at a sports match.Accountant: Accountants handle money, but they work in offices, not the field of play.
Jobs at a sports match.Florist: Florists sell flowers, and have no place on the match day staff.
Jobs at a sports match.Lawyer: Lawyers argue cases in courts; some sports have tribunals, but they aren't part of a match.
Jobs at a sports match.Bank teller: Tellers handle deposits at a bank, not at a sports match.
Jobs at a sports match.Optician: Opticians test eyesight and make glasses; no official role on match day.
Jobs at a sports match.Chimney sweep: Chimney sweeps clean flues, and by tradition are lucky at weddings, not matches.
Jobs at a sports match.Locksmith: Locksmiths open locks, which doesn't fit a match staff.

Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Bowline: Called the king of knots, it makes a fixed loop that will not slip or jam. Sailors and rescuers trust it, and it unties easily even after heavy loads.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Reef knot: Used to tie in the reef points of a sail, hence the name. It is great for bandages but unsafe for heavy loads because it can capsize.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Clove hitch: A quick hitch for tying a rope to a post or rail. It's fast to tie and adjust, but it can slip if the load changes direction.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Sheet bend: A knot for joining two ropes, especially of different thickness. Sailors used it to attach a sheet, the line that controls a sail, to a sail.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Figure eight: A stopper knot that keeps a rope from running through a fitting. Climbers also use a version of it to tie into their harness.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Granny knot: A reef knot tied wrongly, with the second half crossed the wrong way. It is the notorious trap here: it looks right but slips under strain.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Slip knot: A loop that tightens as you pull on the free end. It is easily released by tugging the other end, which makes it handy for temporary ties.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Half hitch: A simple turn of rope around an object. One alone is weak, but two half hitches in a row make a dependable way to secure a line.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Sheepshank: A knot for shortening a rope without cutting it. It only holds while under tension, so it's wise to add extra turns for safety.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Square knot: Another name for the reef knot. Its symmetry makes it look tidy, and it is traditionally used in first aid.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Monkey's fist: A ball-shaped knot at the end of a throwing line that adds weight. Sailors tie one to heave a light line to a dock or other ship.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Taut-line hitch: An adjustable loop that grips under tension, popular for tent guy lines. You can slide it to tighten, and it holds when you let go.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Half nelson: A wrestling hold where one arm is driven under the opponent's arm to the neck. It involves a body, not a rope.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Full nelson: A wrestling hold with both arms under the opponent's armpits, hands locked behind the neck. It's a body grip, not a knot.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Headlock: A hold where one arm wraps around the opponent's head. Wrestlers use it often, but sailors use rope instead of arms.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Suplex: A throwing move in wrestling where you lift and slam your opponent backward. It's a move, with no relation to knotted rope.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Cartwheel: A gymnastic move in which you rotate sideways on hands and feet. It is a trick, so it will not hold a boat to a dock.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Pirouette: A ballet turn on one foot, from the French for spinning top. It is a dance step, not a rope tie.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Pretzel: A baked snack in a looped shape, said to look like arms crossed in prayer. It resembles a knot but it's one you eat.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Cat's cradle: A string game in which a loop is passed between fingers to form patterns. It uses string, but it isn't a true knot, since it has no tie.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Macrame: A craft of decorative knotting for wall hangings and plant hangers. Though it uses knots, it isn't one itself.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Kickflip: A skateboard trick in which the board flips under the feet. Tony Hawk's era made it a classic of street skating.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Ollie: A skateboard jump invented by Alan Gelfand around 1978, popping the board into the air without hands. It's the base of most tricks.
Knots you'd learn in scouting or sailing.Nutmeg: In soccer, passing the ball between an opponent's legs. The slang may come from 'nut' referring to testicles, not the spice, though the origin is debated.

Viking Age words.Longship: Its shallow hull let raiders sail the open ocean, then land straight onto beaches. The Oseberg ship, buried in about 834, survives.
Viking Age words.Runes: The runic alphabet is called the futhark, after the sounds of its first six letters.
Viking Age words.Mead: Honey wine is among humanity's oldest drinks. In Norse myth, a magic mead gave whoever drank it the gift of poetry.
Viking Age words.Saga: These prose tales were mostly written in Iceland in the 1200s, long after the events they describe.
Viking Age words.Jarl: A noble or chieftain rank. The English word earl descends from it.
Viking Age words.Skald: A court poet who praised kings in intricate verse. Skalds were the Vikings' memory keepers and publicists.
Viking Age words.Berserker: A fierce warrior said to fight in a frenzy, perhaps named for bear-skin shirts. English took go berserk from them.
Viking Age words.Valhalla: Odin's hall, where warriors chosen by the Valkyries feast and fight until Ragnarok, the end of the world.
Viking Age words.Vinland: The land Leif Erikson's crew reached around 1000. The Norse site L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is its likely echo.
Viking Age words.Thrall: An enslaved person at the bottom of Viking society. English enthrall comes from the same word.
Viking Age words.Shield wall: A close line of overlapping shields. Vikings and Anglo-Saxons used it, and it nearly decided the Battle of Hastings.
Viking Age words.Longhouse: A communal dwelling with a central hearth, its smoke escaping through a roof hole. It housed family, servants and sometimes animals.
Viking Age words.Horned helmet: A myth. No Viking helmet with horns has ever been found, and the image comes from 19th-century opera costumes.
Viking Age words.Samurai: Japan's warrior class, from a different part of the world. Samurai and Vikings never met.
Viking Age words.Gladiator: A Roman arena fighter from centuries before the Viking Age, and from a very different world.
Viking Age words.Toga: Roman citizen's dress, long out of fashion by the Viking Age. Norse people wore wool tunics and cloaks.
Viking Age words.Pharaoh: Egypt's rulers lived thousands of years earlier. The Great Pyramid was already over 3,000 years old when Vikings first sailed.
Viking Age words.Centurion: A Roman army officer commanding about 80 men. Rome's western empire had fallen centuries before Vikings raided.
Viking Age words.Musket: Gunpowder muskets came centuries after the Viking Age. Vikings fought with axes, spears and swords.
Viking Age words.Legion: A Roman army unit of several thousand soldiers. Vikings fought in warbands, not legions.
Viking Age words.Sombrero: A Mexican wide-brimmed hat; the word comes from Spanish for shade. Vikings never reached Mexico.
Viking Age words.Tomahawk: A word from an Algonquian language of North America, for a Native American axe. Not Norse.
Viking Age words.Igloo: An Inuit word for a house; only some Inuit built snow ones. Norse Greenlanders met Inuit ancestors late, but never used it.
Viking Age words.Kimono: Japan's traditional robe, and a word from another continent. It has no Viking connection.

What a knight needs for a joust.Lance: A long wooden spear held under the arm. Jousting lances were often hollow and designed to splinter on impact, so a hit looked dramatic but spared the rider.
What a knight needs for a joust.Warhorse: A big, strong horse bred for carrying a rider in full armor. Its weight is a myth-sized legend, but the heavier 'destrier' was prized above all others.
What a knight needs for a joust.Shield: Often painted with heraldic arms. In a joust it was tilted to deflect a lance, and a hit could still unseat the rider.
What a knight needs for a joust.Helm: A steel head covering with a narrow slot to see through. In the joust, a special heavier 'great helm' was bolted to the breastplate.
What a knight needs for a joust.Plate armor: Full steel suits weighed roughly 20 to 25 kg, spread across the body, so wearers could still move and even mount without help.
What a knight needs for a joust.Saddle: Jousting saddles had tall cantles that braced the knight, so the lance's impact would push rider and horse together rather than knock him off.
What a knight needs for a joust.Squire: A young knight-in-training who carried gear and armed his master. Squires often trained for years before being knighted.
What a knight needs for a joust.Spurs: Knights wore these on their heels, and being 'awarded one's spurs' meant being knighted. Gold spurs marked a knight.
What a knight needs for a joust.Gauntlets: Armoured gloves, said to be the origin of the phrase 'throw down the gauntlet' to challenge someone.
What a knight needs for a joust.Breastplate: Armour covering the torso. At tournaments, it was often reinforced extra thick on the left, where lances struck.
What a knight needs for a joust.Javelin: Trap: a light throwing spear used by ancient soldiers and athletes, thrown rather than couched in a joust.
What a knight needs for a joust.Trident: Trap: a three-pronged spear of the sea god Poseidon and of Roman gladiators. Not used by jousting knights.
What a knight needs for a joust.Net: Trap: Roman gladiators called retiarii fought with nets and tridents. Knights in tournaments used none of that.
What a knight needs for a joust.Chariot: Trap: a two-wheeled ancient vehicle used in war and races, and a very different era from medieval knights.
What a knight needs for a joust.Boxing gloves: Trap: padded gloves for boxing, a sport with rules developed in 19th-century England, nowhere near a medieval tournament.
What a knight needs for a joust.Tennis racket: Trap: tennis rackets grew out of medieval hand-tennis, but a joust had nothing to do with them.
What a knight needs for a joust.Hockey stick: Trap: sticks for ice or field hockey, games that came much later. No joust involved one.
What a knight needs for a joust.Baseball bat: Trap: baseball developed in America in the 1800s, many centuries after the age of jousts.
What a knight needs for a joust.Golf club: Trap: golf became popular in 15th-century Scotland, but its clubs play no part in a knight's tournament.
What a knight needs for a joust.Basketball: Trap: invented in 1891 by James Naismith as an indoor winter game, long after tournaments ended.
What a knight needs for a joust.Referee whistle: Trap: whistles for referees date from the 1800s. A joust had heralds and marshals instead.
What a knight needs for a joust.Polo mallet: Trap: a horseback sport with a similar spirit and Persian origin, but not a knight's tool.
What a knight needs for a joust.Skateboard: Trap: invented in California in the 1950s. A joust has no wheels beyond the horse's cart.
What a knight needs for a joust.Surfboard: Trap: surfing began in Polynesia, and has nothing to do with medieval European knights.

Things that need ink to work.Ballpoint pen: Its tiny rolling ball, often made from tungsten carbide, is about 1 millimeter wide, and it drags a thick oil-based ink over the page.
Things that need ink to work.Printer: Inkjet printers fire microscopic droplets of ink, each far smaller than a speck of dust, thousands of times per second.
Things that need ink to work.Fountain pen: A fountain pen's nib is split so ink flows down by capillary action, and the metal tip is often tipped with a hard alloy.
Things that need ink to work.Stamp pad: The pad is a block of ink-soaked felt or foam that coats the rubber stamp evenly with each press.
Things that need ink to work.Marker: A permanent marker's ink uses fast-drying solvents, and that is why the smell is so strong and the lines are hard to wash off.
Things that need ink to work.Typewriter: A typewriter strikes letters through an inked ribbon onto paper, and the ribbon is typically a long fabric strip.
Things that need ink to work.Highlighter: Highlighter ink is translucent and fluorescent, so you can read text through it, which is why it is used for study.
Things that need ink to work.Rubber stamp: Without ink, a rubber stamp leaves only an invisible dent, and some are self-inking, with a built-in pad.
Things that need ink to work.Gel pen: Gel pens use a water-based gel that is thicker than ordinary ink, and they came to the market in the 1980s in Japan.
Things that need ink to work.Quill pen: A quill is a bird's feather, usually a goose's, and it was the main writing tool in the West for over a thousand years.
Things that need ink to work.Pencil: A pencil needs no ink, and its mark comes from layers of graphite rubbed onto paper, and no lead is actually involved.
Things that need ink to work.Crayon: A crayon draws with colored wax and pigment, and no ink flows, which is why it works so well on rough paper.
Things that need ink to work.Chalk: Chalk is a soft stone, a form of limestone, and blackboard chalk is these days often made from gypsum.
Things that need ink to work.Eraser: An eraser removes marks rather than making them, so no ink is needed, though special ones can erase ink.
Things that need ink to work.Charcoal: Charcoal is burnt wood, often willow, that leaves a dark powdery line, and artists have used it for thousands of years.
Things that need ink to work.Colored pencil: A colored pencil has a core of pigment and wax or oil, and no liquid ink is involved.
Things that need ink to work.Oil pastel: An oil pastel is pigment mixed with oil and wax, so it is an ink-free drawing tool that stays creamy and soft.
Things that need ink to work.Calculator: A calculator needs only battery or solar power, and a display, so it doesn't use ink at all.
Things that need ink to work.Scissors: Scissors cut by shearing and need no ink, and ink only comes into play if you are cutting up a printout.
Things that need ink to work.Paintbrush: A paintbrush needs paint, not ink, and a good brush can be made from sable, squirrel, or synthetic fibers.
Things that need ink to work.Glue stick: A glue stick works by sticking, not writing, and its purple glue goes on colored and then dries clear.
Things that need ink to work.Ruler: A ruler just guides a line and needs no ink of its own, and the oldest rulers date back thousands of years.
Things that need ink to work.Etch A Sketch: It draws by scraping a line through aluminum powder behind the glass, so no ink is used at all.
Things that need ink to work.Whiteboard eraser: It wipes dry-erase marker off a board, and takes ink away instead of using any to work.

Parts of an animal cell.Nucleus: The nucleus holds the cell's DNA, and it's usually the largest structure in an animal cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Mitochondria: Mitochondria make most of the cell's energy as ATP, and they carry their own small DNA, inherited from your mother.
Parts of an animal cell.Ribosome: Ribosomes build proteins from instructions copied from DNA, and one cell can contain millions.
Parts of an animal cell.Cytoplasm: The cytoplasm is the jelly-like fluid filling the cell, and it's where much of the cell's chemistry happens.
Parts of an animal cell.Cell membrane: The cell membrane is a thin double layer of fat that controls what goes in and out of the cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Golgi apparatus: The Golgi apparatus packs and ships proteins, and it's named for Camillo Golgi, who discovered it in 1898.
Parts of an animal cell.Lysosome: Lysosomes are the cell's recycling centers, full of enzymes that break down waste.
Parts of an animal cell.Centriole: Centrioles are small tubes that help divide the cell, and they come as a pair.
Parts of an animal cell.Nucleolus: The nucleolus is a dense spot inside the nucleus where ribosomes are assembled.
Parts of an animal cell.Chromosome: Chromosomes are tightly coiled DNA, and humans normally have 46 in each cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Chloroplast: Chloroplasts belong to plant cells and capture light for photosynthesis, so animal cells lack them.
Parts of an animal cell.Cell wall: A cell wall is a tough outer layer found in plants and fungi, and animal cells don't have one.
Parts of an animal cell.Neutron: A neutron is a subatomic particle, and it's far smaller than a cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Proton: A proton is a positively charged particle in an atom, not a cell part.
Parts of an animal cell.Electron: An electron is a tiny negatively charged particle in an atom, and not part of a cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Quark: A quark is a building block of protons and neutrons, so it's much smaller than a cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Alveolus: An alveolus is a tiny air sac in the lung, and it is made up of cells, but it isn't a cell part.
Parts of an animal cell.Photon: A photon is a particle of light, and not a cell part.
Parts of an animal cell.Isotope: An isotope is a version of an element with a different number of neutrons, so it's physics, not biology.
Parts of an animal cell.Capillary: A capillary is a tiny blood vessel built of cells, not a part inside a cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Tendon: A tendon is a tissue joining muscle to bone, much bigger than a cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Femur: The femur is a bone, far larger than any cell.
Parts of an animal cell.Nebula: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space, which is a whole different scale.
Parts of an animal cell.Orbital: An orbital is the region where an electron is likely to be found in an atom, and it's not a cell part.

Things you should never lick.Battery: Licking a battery gives a tingle because saliva completes a circuit, but a swallowed or damaged cell can leak harsh chemicals.
Things you should never lick.Frozen flagpole: A frozen flagpole is the 'A Christmas Story' dare: wet tongue freezes onto cold metal, since moisture turns to ice at the contact.
Things you should never lick.Cactus: Cactus spines are modified leaves, and even if you dodge them, tiny barbed hairs called glochids can lodge in your tongue.
Things you should never lick.Slug: Slugs wrap themselves in mucus, and in some regions they carry rat lungworm, a parasite that can seriously harm people.
Things you should never lick.Poison ivy: Poison ivy's oil, urushiol, causes an itchy rash on a tiny amount, and an oily lick of leaf could swell your mouth and throat.
Things you should never lick.Cane toad: Cane toads secrete toxin from glands behind their eyes, and licking one can cause real poisoning, hence the tale of 'toad-licking'.
Things you should never lick.Hot iron: A hot iron can reach 200 C or more, so licking one can scald your tongue in an instant, long before you know it.
Things you should never lick.Mousetrap: A mousetrap's spring snaps in a fraction of a second, and a tongue is far more painful than a mouse's whiskers.
Things you should never lick.Stinging nettle: Stinging nettle hairs break like tiny needles and inject irritants, though boiling or drying the plant makes it safe to eat.
Things you should never lick.Jellyfish: Jellyfish tentacles carry stinging cells that fire without the animal deciding, and some can even sting after the creature is dead.
Things you should never lick.Ice cream cone: Ice cream cones were popularized at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, and licking them is the entire point.
Things you should never lick.Lollipop: Lollipops are made to be licked, and the name may come from a Romani word, though its true origin is disputed.
Things you should never lick.Envelope: A trap: licking an envelope is the classic way to seal one, but the gum is food-safe, and many modern ones are self-adhesive.
Things you should never lick.Stamp: Stamps were once licked to stick, and the gum on the back of a traditional stamp is a mild, edible adhesive.
Things you should never lick.Popsicle: Popsicles were accidentally invented in 1905 by 11-year-old Frank Epperson, who left a soda drink with a stick out overnight.
Things you should never lick.Spoon: A spoon is the classic tool for licking clean, and for centuries spoons were carved from wood or horn before metal ones spread.
Things you should never lick.Frosting: Frosting is sweet butter and sugar, and licking the beater is a cherished kitchen tradition for cooks everywhere.
Things you should never lick.Candy cane: Candy canes are said to date to 1670, when a choirmaster in Germany bent sugar sticks for children during a church service.
Things you should never lick.Chocolate bar: Chocolate bars are fair to lick, and it melts at about 34 C, just below your body temperature.
Things you should never lick.Peanut butter: Peanut butter licked from a spoon is a favorite, and peanuts aren't nuts at all, but legumes related to peas.
Things you should never lick.Cotton candy: Cotton candy was popularized at the 1904 World's Fair, and a dentist helped invent the machine that spun sugar into floss.
Things you should never lick.Yogurt lid: Licking the yogurt lid is a beloved habit, and some brands even marketed their foil lids as the best part of the cup.
Things you should never lick.Honey: Honey is safe and sweet to lick, and a jar of it can last for centuries, since few microbes can survive in it.
Things you should never lick.Jam: Jam is a classic licking treat, and it sets thanks to pectin, a natural fiber found in fruit, especially its peels.

Farm machinery.Tractor: The word comes from Latin for 'pulling'. Early tractors were steam-driven, and gasoline models only took over farms in the early 1900s.
Farm machinery.Combine harvester: It earned its name by combining reaping, threshing and winnowing in one pass, jobs that once took whole crews of workers.
Farm machinery.Plough: Among the oldest farm tools, ploughs were drawn by oxen thousands of years ago. Spelled 'plow' in American English.
Farm machinery.Baler: It squeezes loose hay or straw into tight bundles. Modern round balers can make bales weighing close to a ton.
Farm machinery.Seed drill: Jethro Tull's horse-drawn version of about 1701 planted seeds in neat rows at set depth, helping spark Britain's agricultural revolution.
Farm machinery.Harrow: Dragged behind a tractor after ploughing, its spikes or discs break up clods. 'Harrowing' as a word for distressing comes from the same tool.
Farm machinery.Cultivator: Its tines stir soil between crop rows to uproot weeds without chemicals. Cultivating a skill borrows the farming idea.
Farm machinery.Hay rake: It gathers cut grass into long windrows so it dries evenly and a baler can scoop it up neatly.
Farm machinery.Crop sprayer: Some modern sprayers use cameras to spot individual weeds and squirt only those, cutting herbicide use dramatically.
Farm machinery.Muck spreader: It flings manure across fields as fertilizer. Farmers have recycled animal waste this way for thousands of years.
Farm machinery.Bulldozer: Its fame comes from pushing earth, but it is construction kit, not farm machinery. The name probably began as slang for a heavy dose of coercion.
Farm machinery.Forklift: Warehouses, not farms, are its home turf. It balances its load using a heavy rear counterweight, like a seesaw.
Farm machinery.Crane: Cranes hoist loads on building sites and ports. Ancient Greeks already used them, powered by people running in treadmill wheels.
Farm machinery.Excavator: A construction digger that fits no field routine. Its arm mimics a human arm with a shoulder, elbow and wrist-like bucket joint.
Farm machinery.Steamroller: It flattens roads, not fields. The roller's sheer weight, often over ten tons, compacts hot asphalt into a smooth surface.
Farm machinery.Snowplow: Built to clear roads in winter, it is road equipment. Some cities name their plows through public contests.
Farm machinery.Tank: A battlefield vehicle. The name came from a wartime cover story in 1915 that called the secret new machines water tanks.
Farm machinery.Golf cart: Though common on courses, it isn't farm gear. Many retirement communities now rely on them as everyday transport.
Farm machinery.Jackhammer: A hand-held pneumatic tool for breaking concrete, not for fields. The same device is called a pneumatic drill in Britain.
Farm machinery.Ambulance: Its name comes from Latin for 'walking', since early ones were field hospitals that moved with armies, not vehicles for the sick.
Farm machinery.Zamboni: Frank Zamboni built the first ice resurfacer in 1949 for his California ice rink. It belongs at rinks, not on farms.
Farm machinery.Segway: This two-wheeled scooter balances using gyroscopes, and is a personal transporter. It has no work on farms.
Farm machinery.Hovercraft: It rides on a cushion of air and crossed the English Channel in 1959. It glides over water and marsh, but it's no farm tool.
Farm machinery.Tram: A rail or street vehicle for carrying passengers through cities. Lisbon and Melbourne are famous for their trams, not for any farm use.

US Army ranks.Private: The entry rank of the US Army. Its name comes from the old idea of a 'private soldier' with no title or office.
US Army ranks.Corporal: Corporals are the lowest non-commissioned officers. The name comes from Italian for 'head', as they led a small squad.
US Army ranks.Sergeant: Sergeants run the Army day to day, and the word comes from Latin 'servant'. The title has roots in medieval household service.
US Army ranks.Lieutenant: The word means 'place-holder' in French, as in someone standing in for a superior. Americans say 'loo-TEN-ant', Britons 'lef-TEN-ant'.
US Army ranks.Captain: In the US Army a captain often commands a company of 100 or so soldiers. The Navy uses the same word for a far higher rank.
US Army ranks.Major: Ranks above captain and below lieutenant colonel. Oddly, a major outranks a lieutenant but a major general ranks above a brigadier general.
US Army ranks.Colonel: Pronounced 'kernel', a spelling quirk from the Italian and French forms. Colonels commonly lead a regiment or brigade.
US Army ranks.General: Full 'four-star' generals are the Army's top peacetime rank. The only five-star generals were made during World War II.
US Army ranks.Specialist: A rank for soldiers with technical skills but no command role. It sits between private and sergeant in the pay scale.
US Army ranks.Brigadier General: A one-star general who often serves as a deputy commander of a division. The Army sometimes calls them 'one-stars'.
US Army ranks.Admiral: This is a Navy rank. The word comes from Arabic 'amir al-', meaning commander of the sea.
US Army ranks.Commodore: Rarely used in modern US service, it was a Navy rank between captain and rear admiral. It's naval, not army.
US Army ranks.Ensign: The lowest commissioned Navy officer. The word once meant a flag bearer, so Army ensigns carried the colors in battle.
US Army ranks.Petty Officer: A Navy enlisted rank, not an Army one. 'Petty' comes from French 'petit', meaning small or minor.
US Army ranks.Midshipman: A naval academy student, named for where early trainees worked: amidships. No Army rank carries this name.
US Army ranks.Bosun: A ship's officer in charge of crew and deck equipment. Short for 'boatswain', which sounds nothing like it's spelled.
US Army ranks.Sheriff: An elected county law officer, not a soldier. The word started as 'shire reeve', the king's agent over an English county.
US Army ranks.Marshal: A law enforcement officer or, in some nations, a top military title. US Marshals are federal officers, not Army.
US Army ranks.Constable: A police rank used in Britain and elsewhere. It comes from Latin for 'count of the stable', a medieval court officer.
US Army ranks.Detective: A police investigator. The term emerged in the 1840s alongside the first police detective units in London.
US Army ranks.Inspector: A police rank in many countries, not an Army one. Ironically, Sherlock Holmes stories mock Scotland Yard inspectors.
US Army ranks.Commander: A Navy rank above lieutenant commander. Army soldiers say a 'commander' for a role, not as a specific grade.
US Army ranks.Chancellor: A government or university head, not military. Germany's leader still holds this title.
US Army ranks.Pharaoh: Ancient Egypt's ruler. The word originally meant 'great house', referring to the palace rather than the king.

Things a blacksmith uses.Anvil: Traditional anvils weigh anywhere from about 50 to over 150 kilograms, and the heavy mass makes each hammer blow count.
Things a blacksmith uses.Forge: A forge heats iron to a glowing orange of over 1,000 degrees Celsius so it can be shaped.
Things a blacksmith uses.Tongs: Smiths use tongs of many shapes, each fitted to hold a specific shape of hot metal.
Things a blacksmith uses.Bellows: Bellows pump air into the fire, raising the temperature far above a plain wood fire.
Things a blacksmith uses.Hammer: A smith's hammer is balanced for hours of swinging, and the ring of hammer on anvil is a classic sound of the trade.
Things a blacksmith uses.Coal: Smiths prefer coal or coke for forges because it burns hotter and cleaner than wood.
Things a blacksmith uses.Leather apron: A thick leather apron shields against sparks and hot scale, and was a trademark of the trade.
Things a blacksmith uses.Quenching bucket: Dunking hot steel in water or oil cools it fast and hardens it, a step called quenching.
Things a blacksmith uses.Vise: The big leg vise is bolted to a post, and it can take heavy hammering while gripping a piece.
Things a blacksmith uses.Swage block: A swage block is a heavy slab with grooves and holes used to shape metal into rounds and other forms.
Things a blacksmith uses.Kiln: A kiln fires pottery and bricks, so it's a potter's heat source, not a smith's.
Things a blacksmith uses.Loom: A loom weaves cloth, so it's the tool of a weaver.
Things a blacksmith uses.Easel: An easel props up a painter's canvas, and it's wooden and light, the opposite of a smith's heavy iron kit.
Things a blacksmith uses.Whisk: A whisk beats air into eggs and cream in a kitchen, and a smith's only whisking is the quench bucket's splash.
Things a blacksmith uses.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is for listening to hearts, which makes it a doctor's tool.
Things a blacksmith uses.Thimble: A thimble guards a sewing finger, so it's a tailor's tool.
Things a blacksmith uses.Potter's wheel: It spins clay into pots, so it belongs to a potter.
Things a blacksmith uses.Plunger: A plunger is a plumber's tool for clearing drains.
Things a blacksmith uses.Stapler: A stapler is an office tool, and the smith's equivalent would be nails or rivets.
Things a blacksmith uses.Pinking shears: Pinking shears give a zigzag edge to cloth, so they belong to a seamstress.
Things a blacksmith uses.Spinning wheel: A spinning wheel makes yarn, so it is a textile tool.
Things a blacksmith uses.Typewriter: A typewriter is for writing, and no smith would put it near sparks.
Things a blacksmith uses.Microscope: A microscope is for tiny things in a lab, though metallurgists do study steel under one.
Things a blacksmith uses.Paintbrush: A paintbrush belongs to an artist, and a smith uses a hammer instead.

Things a bricklayer uses.Trowel: A skilled bricklayer can flick mortar into place with a single motion, laying hundreds of bricks in a day.
Things a bricklayer uses.Mortar: Mortar glues bricks together and spreads the load between them; the word also names a bowl for crushing spices.
Things a bricklayer uses.Bricks: A standard British brick is 215 millimeters long, sized so one hand can lift it while the other holds the trowel.
Things a bricklayer uses.Spirit level: A bubble in a liquid-filled vial centers when a surface is level, an idea from the 1660s credited to Melchisedech Thevenot.
Things a bricklayer uses.Brick hammer: One end is flat for tapping, the other chisel-shaped for cutting bricks to fit.
Things a bricklayer uses.Jointer: It shapes the mortar joint, and a concave profile sheds rain well.
Things a bricklayer uses.Mortarboard: Not just a graduation cap: bricklayers hold mortar on a flat board, and the hat is named after it.
Things a bricklayer uses.Plumb line: A weight on a string uses gravity to check vertical walls, and Egyptians used them in pyramid building.
Things a bricklayer uses.Scaffolding: Bamboo scaffolding is still used on skyscrapers in Hong Kong.
Things a bricklayer uses.String line: A line stretched between corners keeps every course of bricks straight and level.
Things a bricklayer uses.Stethoscope: The two-earpiece version, with flexible tubes, arrived in the 1850s.
Things a bricklayer uses.Whisk: Whisks beat air into food; mortar mixers use a paddle instead.
Things a bricklayer uses.Easel: Artists use easels for paintings, and the word comes from a Dutch term meaning donkey.
Things a bricklayer uses.Plunger: A plumber's rubber cup that unclogs drains, not a mason's tool.
Things a bricklayer uses.Scalpel: A surgeon's blade, designed for precision, not for cutting bricks.
Things a bricklayer uses.Thimble: A thimble protects a seamstress's finger, and some bricklayers wear gloves instead.
Things a bricklayer uses.Rolling pin: A baker's tool for flattening dough, nothing like a mason's wall.
Things a bricklayer uses.Pinking shears: Zigzag-edged scissors for fabric, so cloth edges do not fray.
Things a bricklayer uses.Lasso: A ranch rope loop, and the word comes from the Spanish lazo.
Things a bricklayer uses.Fishing rod: An angler's flexible rod, not a rigid builder's tool.
Things a bricklayer uses.Bellows: A blacksmith's air pump for the fire, though bricklayers do not forge.
Things a bricklayer uses.Microscope: A lab tool for tiny things; bricklayers work with much larger objects.
Things a bricklayer uses.Paint roller: A painter's tool, since brick walls are normally left unpainted.
Things a bricklayer uses.Stapler: A desk tool for papers; the first mass-produced staplers came in the late 19th century.

Jobs in a newsroom.Editor: An editor decides what runs and what gets cut; at big papers the editor-in-chief also carries legal responsibility for content.
Jobs in a newsroom.Reporter: Most news stories use the inverted pyramid, putting the key facts first so editors can trim from the bottom.
Jobs in a newsroom.Journalist: The word comes from French journal, meaning daily, and the job now spans print, broadcast and online.
Jobs in a newsroom.Photographer: Robert Capa's D-Day photos survived largely by accident; a darkroom mishap melted most of the film.
Jobs in a newsroom.Copy editor: They fix grammar and style and write headlines and captions, as the last line of defence against errors.
Jobs in a newsroom.Columnist: The name comes from the column of the printed page where their regular opinion piece appears.
Jobs in a newsroom.News anchor: The term gained fame at the 1952 US conventions, when CBS used an 'anchor' to hold its coverage together.
Jobs in a newsroom.Fact-checker: Magazines such as The New Yorker keep dedicated fact-checkers who verify names, dates and quotes before publication.
Jobs in a newsroom.Correspondent: Literally someone who corresponds, or writes letters, from far away, as early foreign correspondents did.
Jobs in a newsroom.Sub-editor: The British word for the person who tightens stories, checks style and writes headlines, 'subs' for short.
Jobs in a newsroom.Bailiff: A court officer who keeps order; in medieval England, a bailiff also managed a lord's estate.
Jobs in a newsroom.Croupier: A casino dealer; the word is French for the rider behind on a horse's croup.
Jobs in a newsroom.Sommelier: A restaurant's wine expert; the French word comes from an old term for a pack-animal driver.
Jobs in a newsroom.Farrier: Trims hooves and fits horseshoes; the word comes from Latin ferrum, meaning iron.
Jobs in a newsroom.Midwife: Literally 'with woman' in Old English, and midwives have assisted births for thousands of years.
Jobs in a newsroom.Shepherd: Tends sheep; dogs such as border collies do much of the herding work.
Jobs in a newsroom.Lumberjack: Fells trees, and logger competitions such as log rolling and axe throwing still draw crowds.
Jobs in a newsroom.Jockey: Rides racehorses; jockeys are small, often weighing only 50 to 55 kilograms.
Jobs in a newsroom.Bellhop: Carries guests' bags at a hotel; the name came from the bell on the front desk used to summon them.
Jobs in a newsroom.Golf caddie: Carries a golfer's bag and advises on the course; the word is thought to come from French cadet.
Jobs in a newsroom.Lifeguard: A lifeguard trains to spot a drowning person, who is often silent rather than shouting.
Jobs in a newsroom.Usher: The word comes from Latin ostiarius, meaning doorkeeper, and the job still guards entrances.
Jobs in a newsroom.Dentist: The first dental school, the Baltimore College of Dental Surgery, opened in 1840.
Jobs in a newsroom.Gondolier: Steers a Venetian gondola, an asymmetric boat built to lean and counter the one-sided rowing.

Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iPhone: Steve Jobs unveiled it in January 2007 as three devices in one: a widescreen iPod, a phone and an internet communicator.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iPad: Apple had a tablet in development before the iPhone, then reused its multitouch technology for the phone first; the iPad arrived in 2010.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iMac: The 1998 original came in translucent Bondi blue and ditched the floppy drive; the 'i' stood for internet.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iPod: The first one, in 2001, promised '1,000 songs in your pocket' on a 5 GB hard drive.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iTunes: It grew out of SoundJam, a Mac player Apple bought in 2000, and was retired in 2019 in favor of separate apps.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iCloud: Launched in 2011 as the replacement for the troubled MobileMe, it gives every account 5 GB of free storage.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iMessage: Launched in 2011; blue bubbles mean an Apple-to-Apple chat, while green means it fell back to plain SMS.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iMovie: Debuted in 1999 on the iMac DV, bringing desktop video editing to ordinary home users.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iBook: Also the name of Apple's colorful 1999 clamshell laptop, which had a built-in carry handle, before it became the books app.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iOS: Originally named iPhone OS, it was renamed iOS in 2010, around the time of iOS 4.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iPadOS: Split off from iOS in 2019 so the iPad could have its own features, such as better multitasking.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iWork: Apple's office suite of Pages, Numbers and Keynote; Keynote began as the software Steve Jobs used for his own presentations.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iRobot: The Roomba maker was founded by MIT roboticists in 1990; the name nods to Isaac Asimov's I, Robot.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iRiver: A South Korean MP3 player maker that competed head-on with the iPod in the 2000s.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iHeartRadio: Streaming service from iHeartMedia, the radio giant once known as Clear Channel; it has nothing to do with Apple.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iPlayer: The BBC's catch-up streaming service, launched in 2007, was a pioneer of watching TV on demand.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iCarly: A Nickelodeon sitcom from 2007 about a web show; its title just borrows the iPod-era naming style.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iDrive: BMW's infotainment control system, introduced in 2001 around a single rotary knob; the name has been reused for a backup service too.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.IHOP: The International House of Pancakes briefly renamed itself IHOb in 2018 as a burger stunt. No relation to Apple.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iGoogle: Google's customizable homepage, which launched in 2005 and was shut down in 2013.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iStock: A stock photo site founded in 1999 that was bought by Getty Images in 2006.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iBuyPower: A California gaming PC builder; its name copied Apple's 'i' trend, but it's no Apple product.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.iFixit: Known for teardown reviews and repair guides, it scores gadgets on how fixable they are.
Apple products and apps starting with 'i.Inkscape: A free, open-source vector graphics editor with no Apple link, even though the name begins with I.

Game franchises owned by Microsoft.World of Warcraft: Blizzard's 2004 online role-playing game once had over 12 million subscribers, and it's now Microsoft's.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Fallout: Bethesda took over the post-apocalyptic series in 2007, and Microsoft got it by buying ZeniMax in 2021. An Amazon TV show followed.

Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Doom: id Software's shooter belongs to Microsoft via ZeniMax, and the original famously ran on everything from calculators to pregnancy tests.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Candy Crush: King created it in 2012, and as a part of Activision Blizzard it joined Microsoft in 2023.

Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Mario: Nintendo's plumber isn't Microsoft's, though the two companies have a long relationship with Minecraft on Switch.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Zelda: The princess, not the green-clad hero, gives the series its name, honoring Zelda Fitzgerald. In Ocarina of Time she hides as Sheik.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Pokémon: Owned by The Pokémon Company, in which Nintendo, Game Freak and Creatures hold stakes, so not Microsoft's.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Sonic: Sega's blue mascot is not Microsoft's, though Sonic games have appeared on Xbox consoles, as with many others.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Grand Theft Auto: Rockstar Games' crime series is owned by Take-Two, so it isn't Microsoft's, though it remains one of the best-selling franchises ever.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.FIFA: The football series long belonged to EA and was renamed EA Sports FC in 2023 after a licensing split, so it's not Microsoft's.
Game franchises owned by Microsoft.Fortnite: Epic Games' battle royale hit isn't Microsoft's. Epic is privately held, with Tencent as a major investor.

Real Git commands.commit: Records a snapshot of staged changes, and each commit gets a unique hash ID.
Real Git commands.push: It sends your commits to a remote, and a force push can overwrite others' history, so teams often guard against it.
Real Git commands.pull: By default it's a fetch followed by a merge, rolled into one step.
Real Git commands.merge: Combines the histories of two branches, and a conflict arises when both changed the same lines.
Real Git commands.clone: Copies a whole repository including its entire history, so every clone is effectively a full backup.
Real Git commands.branch: Cheap in Git because a branch is simply a pointer to a commit.
Real Git commands.checkout: Switches branches or restores files, and the newer switch and restore commands split up those jobs.
Real Git commands.rebase: Replays your commits onto a new base for a linear history, but it's best avoided on shared branches.
Real Git commands.stash: Shelves uncommitted work temporarily so you can switch tasks and pick it up later.
Real Git commands.fetch: Downloads new data from the remote without touching your files, unlike pull.
Real Git commands.status: Shows which files are changed, staged or untracked, and is the command people run most while unsure.
Real Git commands.log: Lists commit history, and adding --oneline --graph gives a compact view of branches.
Real Git commands.diff: Shows line-by-line differences, borrowing its name and format from the old Unix diff tool.
Real Git commands.save: Not a Git command. Commit records changes, while stash is the closest thing to saving for later.
Real Git commands.upload: Git calls this push, which sends your commits to a remote; upload is the everyday word for it, not the command.
Real Git commands.download: Git has no download command. The closest are fetch and pull.
Real Git commands.sync: Not a command, though people say it; you fetch, pull and push separately.
Real Git commands.send: Not a plain command, though git send-email exists for mailing patches.
Real Git commands.copy: There's no copy command; clone copies a repository, and Git detects copied files on its own.
Real Git commands.undo: There's no undo command. You use revert, reset or restore, and the reflog can rescue commits you thought were lost.
Real Git commands.publish: Some editors show a Publish Branch button, but under the hood it's just git push.
Real Git commands.refresh: Not a command; fetch updates remote information and status checks your files.
Real Git commands.submit: Not a Git command; review tools use that word, but Git itself uses push.
Real Git commands.share: Not a command; you share work by pushing to or pulling from a remote.

Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Icon: The idea of clickable icons came from Xerox PARC research and was popularized by Apple's Lisa and Macintosh in the 1980s.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Cursor: Moved by a mouse, a device Douglas Engelbart publicly demonstrated in 1968 in what became known as the Mother of All Demos.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Taskbar: Windows 95 introduced the taskbar, together with the Start button, and the layout has survived for decades.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Wallpaper: Windows XP's default wallpaper, Bliss, is a photo of a green hillside and is often called one of the most viewed photographs ever.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Folder: The folder icon mimics paper filing, a metaphor carried over from the desktop designs developed at Xerox PARC.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Recycle Bin: Windows' answer to Apple's Trash, an idea that goes back to the Apple Lisa in 1983.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Start button: Windows 95 launched it with a big marketing campaign built around the Rolling Stones' song Start Me Up.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Window: Overlapping windows were pioneered at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, long before they reached ordinary desks.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Scroll bar: The size of its sliding thumb tells you how much of the document you're currently viewing.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Dock: Apple introduced it with Mac OS X, and its icons magnify as the pointer passes over them.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Shortcut: It's a pointer to a file, drawn with a little arrow overlay, and deleting the shortcut leaves the original untouched.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Clock: Computers usually keep it accurate by syncing with internet time servers using NTP, one of the oldest internet protocols.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Resistor: A trap: it's a real part of any computer, but it's hidden inside the machine, so you'll never see it on a desktop screen.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Capacitor: A hidden component inside the machine, and aging ones famously fail in old PCs, swelling up on their motherboards.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Transistor: Billions of them live inside the CPU, doing the switching that makes the desktop possible but remaining invisible.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Diode: An internal electronic part of the computer; on the desktop screen you see only software.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Motherboard: The main circuit board holding everything together is hardware inside the case, not something drawn on screen.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Fan: It cools the machine, and you tend to hear it spinning more than you ever see it on the screen.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Heat sink: Metal fins that pull heat away from the CPU, hidden inside the case, far from the visible desktop.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Power supply: It converts wall AC into the low-voltage DC a PC needs, and it sits inside the case, out of view.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.RAM stick: Temporary memory modules sit inside the computer, and the desktop never draws them on screen.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Hard drive: A trap: the desktop may show an icon of the drive, but the drive itself is hardware inside the machine.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.CPU: It runs everything you see, but it's a chip inside the computer and isn't visible on the desktop.
Things you see on a computer desktop scr.Thermal paste: A paste that fills microscopic gaps between the CPU and its cooler to improve heat flow, hidden inside the case.
