Video game currencies.Robux: Roblox's currency, which creators can cash out into real money, so kids can run a small business.
Video game currencies.Rupees: Zelda's gems of currency, which share a name with the money of India.
Video game currencies.Gil: Final Fantasy's currency, used in nearly every game in the series to buy potions, weapons and inn stays.
Video game currencies.Simoleons: The Sims' money, whose symbol is a section sign, and whose name echoes old slang for a dollar.
Video game currencies.Bells: Animal Crossing's currency, used to pay off Tom Nook's loans, so players always owe someone.
Video game currencies.Bottle caps: Fallout's post-apocalyptic money, where discarded bottle caps are the standard currency.
Video game currencies.Minecoins: Minecraft's real-money currency for buying items on its marketplace, so it isn't mined in the world.
Video game currencies.Zenny: Capcom's currency in Mega Man and Monster Hunter, which appears in several of its series.
Video game currencies.Poké Dollars: Pokemon's money, called the Pokemon Dollar, used to buy Poke Balls and potions.
Video game currencies.Bitcoin: A real cryptocurrency from 2009, not a game's money, though some games accept it.
Video game currencies.Ethereum: A real blockchain and cryptocurrency, not an in-game coin from any game.
Video game currencies.Dogecoin: Started as a 2013 joke based on the Shiba Inu meme, but it's a real cryptocurrency, not a game's coin.
Video game currencies.Galleons: Harry Potter's gold wizard coins come from a book, not a video game, as the other options do.
Video game currencies.Schrute Bucks: The fake money Dwight invented on The Office; it's a TV prop, not a game currency.
Video game currencies.Euro: A real money used in many European countries; digital since 1999 and in notes from 2002.
Video game currencies.Yen: Japan's real currency, whose name means round object, so it's not from a game.
Video game currencies.Peso: A real money used in many countries, like Mexico and Argentina, so it's not game money.
Video game currencies.Franc: Real money; Switzerland still uses the Swiss franc, so it isn't a game currency.
Video game currencies.Drachma: Ancient Greek money and Greece's money until the euro arrived in 2002, so it's not game currency.
Video game currencies.Monopoly money: A board game's money; a standard Monopoly set holds $20,580, and it isn't a video game currency.
Video game currencies.Krona: A real money used in Sweden, Norway and Denmark and Iceland, not an in-game currency.
Video game currencies.Shekel: Israel's real currency, whose name goes back to ancient Mesopotamia, so it's not game money.
Video game currencies.Dinar: Real money used in places like Kuwait, whose dinar is among the world's highest-valued currencies, so it's not game money.

Things traditionally made of wood.Pencil: Most pencils are made of incense cedar, whose soft, even grain sharpens cleanly.
Things traditionally made of wood.Popsicle stick: Popsicle sticks are typically birch, chosen because it's strong, smooth and flavorless.
Things traditionally made of wood.Toothpick: Toothpicks are traditionally birch, and a Boston merchant, Charles Forster, helped make them a US habit in the 1860s.
Things traditionally made of wood.Matchstick: Matchsticks are often aspen or pine, soaked in fire retardant so the stick doesn't keep glowing after it goes out.
Things traditionally made of wood.Violin: Violins use spruce for the top and maple for the back, and some think Stradivari's wood grew slowly during a cold spell.
Things traditionally made of wood.Log cabin: Swedish and Finnish settlers brought log building to America in the 1600s.
Things traditionally made of wood.Wine barrel: Oak wine barrels lend vanilla and spice flavors to the wine.
Things traditionally made of wood.Totem pole: Totem poles are carved from red cedar by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest to record family histories.
Things traditionally made of wood.Cuckoo clock: Cuckoo clocks come from Germany's Black Forest, where woodcarving was a winter craft.
Things traditionally made of wood.Clothespin: The earliest clothespins were forked sticks, and the spring-clip type came along in the 1800s.
Things traditionally made of wood.Rolling pin: A French-style rolling pin has no handles and tapers at the ends, and many bakers prefer it for the feel of the dough.
Things traditionally made of wood.Pinocchio: Pinocchio was carved by Geppetto from a talking log in Carlo Collodi's 1883 book, and his nose grows when he lies.
Things traditionally made of wood.Butcher block: Butcher block is glued strips of hardwood like maple, and end-grain boards are gentler on knives.
Things traditionally made of wood.Soda can: Aluminum cans are infinitely recyclable, and a can can be back on shelves in about two months.
Things traditionally made of wood.Credit card: Modern cards are PVC plastic; early ones were cardboard and paper.
Things traditionally made of wood.Golf ball: Golf balls were once made of wood, then feather-stuffed leather; today they're rubber and plastic with dimples.
Things traditionally made of wood.Window pane: A window's wooden frame is traditional, but the pane itself is glass.
Things traditionally made of wood.Car tire: The Dunlop pneumatic tire was invented in 1888 partly to give a child's tricycle a smoother ride.
Things traditionally made of wood.Coin: Ancient Lydian coins were made of electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy.
Things traditionally made of wood.Candle: Candles are wax, but wooden-wick versions exist that crackle like a fireplace.
Things traditionally made of wood.Balloon: Balloons are latex or foil, never wood, and a latex balloon can be a mere fraction of a millimeter thin.
Things traditionally made of wood.Bottle cap: The crown cork bottle cap has 21 teeth, a design William Painter patented in 1892.
Things traditionally made of wood.Light bulb: Edison's early filaments were carbonized bamboo, but today's bulb is glass and metal, or an LED.
Things traditionally made of wood.Sock: The oldest known knitted socks, from Egypt, date to about a thousand years ago.

Drinks and foods with caffeine.Coffee: Legend says an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi discovered coffee when his goats danced after eating its berries.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Black tea: Black tea has about half the caffeine of coffee per cup, and it's brewed from oxidized leaves.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Green tea: Green and black tea come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis, and differ in processing.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Dark chocolate: A bar of dark chocolate contains caffeine and theobromine, roughly the caffeine of a small cup of coffee.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Coca-Cola: A can of Coca-Cola has about 34 mg of caffeine, roughly a third of a coffee.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Red Bull: A 250 ml can of Red Bull has about 80 mg of caffeine, roughly a cup of coffee.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Espresso: A single espresso shot has about 60 to 65 mg of caffeine, often less than a mug of drip coffee.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Matcha: Matcha is whole powdered green tea leaves, so you consume the entire leaf, and it's shade-grown to boost flavor.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Yerba mate: Yerba mate is a South American drink traditionally shared from a gourd with a metal straw.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Iced tea: Iced tea made from black or green tea has caffeine, and sweet tea is a staple of the American South.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Chai: The word chai simply means tea in Hindi, and masala chai contains black tea, so it has caffeine.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Mountain Dew: Mountain Dew has more caffeine than most sodas, about 54 mg per 12-ounce can.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Chamomile tea: Chamomile tea is a herbal infusion of flowers, and so it has no caffeine at all.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Rooibos: Rooibos comes from a South African bush and is naturally caffeine-free.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Peppermint tea: Peppermint tea is a caffeine-free infusion, a popular remedy for upset stomachs.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Sprite: Sprite is one of the few major sodas with no caffeine, which sets it apart from colas.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.7 Up: 7 Up originally contained lithium citrate, a mood stabilizer, until 1948, but never caffeine.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Orange juice: Orange juice has no caffeine, only plenty of vitamin C.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Milk: Milk has no caffeine, but a latte adds the coffee that does.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Carob: Carob looks and tastes like chocolate without caffeine, and its seeds gave us the word carat.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Fanta: Fanta was created in Germany in 1940 when Coca-Cola syrup became unavailable, and it's caffeine-free.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Ginger ale: Ginger ale is caffeine-free and a traditional remedy for upset stomachs.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Lemonade: Lemonade is caffeine-free, a mix of lemon, water and sugar.
Drinks and foods with caffeine.Sparkling water: Plain sparkling water has no caffeine, only dissolved carbon dioxide.

Things faster than a cheetah.Peregrine falcon: The peregrine is the fastest animal, diving at over 300 km/h, about three times a cheetah's top speed.
Things faster than a cheetah.Bullet train: Japan's Shinkansen opened in 1964 and runs at about 320 km/h, and some maglev trains pass 600.
Things faster than a cheetah.Formula 1 car: An F1 car can go from zero to 200 km/h in under five seconds, and cornering generates multiple g-forces.
Things faster than a cheetah.Jet airliner: Airliners cruise at roughly 900 km/h, which is about eight times a cheetah's sprint.
Things faster than a cheetah.Bullet: A rifle bullet can move at about 900 meters per second, faster than the speed of sound.
Things faster than a cheetah.Space Shuttle: The Space Shuttle orbited at about 28,000 km/h, and it circled the Earth every 90 minutes or so.
Things faster than a cheetah.Lightning: A lightning stroke's channel advances at about a third of the speed of light, much faster than any animal.
Things faster than a cheetah.Sound: Sound travels about 343 meters per second in air, roughly 1,235 km/h, and a cheetah is around a tenth of that.
Things faster than a cheetah.Light: Light moves about 300,000 kilometers per second, and it could circle the Earth about seven times in one second.
Things faster than a cheetah.Tennis serve: The fastest recorded serves exceed 250 km/h, and the ball covers the court in less than half a second.
Things faster than a cheetah.Rocket: A rocket must reach about 28,000 km/h to orbit the Earth, far beyond any cheetah.
Things faster than a cheetah.Thoroughbred horse: Racehorses run about 70 km/h, fast, but a cheetah's 100 km/h top speed still beats them.
Things faster than a cheetah.Greyhound: Greyhounds are the fastest dogs at about 65 km/h, but they can't keep up with a cheetah.
Things faster than a cheetah.Ostrich: An ostrich can sprint about 70 km/h, the fastest on two legs, and sustain it far longer than a cheetah can.
Things faster than a cheetah.Usain Bolt: Bolt's record of 9.58 seconds for 100 meters averages about 37 km/h, with a peak near 44.
Things faster than a cheetah.Pronghorn: The pronghorn can't match the cheetah's top speed but can keep running at about 55 km/h for long distances.
Things faster than a cheetah.Lion: Lions reach about 80 km/h in short bursts, and they're good at ambush rather than long chases.
Things faster than a cheetah.Kangaroo: Red kangaroos can hop at about 70 km/h, and they store energy in their tendons.
Things faster than a cheetah.Dolphin: Dolphins swim at about 30 to 60 km/h, impressive in water but slower than a cheetah on land.
Things faster than a cheetah.Rabbit: Rabbits can run about 50 km/h and zigzag to dodge predators.
Things faster than a cheetah.Bicycle: Racing cyclists hit over 70 km/h in sprints, but a cheetah is faster, and the record is over 280 km/h with a windshield.
Things faster than a cheetah.Skateboard: Downhill skateboarders have passed 140 km/h, but only on special slopes, so a cheetah still outdoes typical riders.
Things faster than a cheetah.Gazelle: Thomson's gazelles reach about 80 km/h and can outlast a cheetah, which tires after short bursts.
Things faster than a cheetah.Zebra: Zebras run about 65 km/h, and their stripes may confuse biting flies rather than lions.

Things on a cruise ship.Buffet: Buffet is French for sideboard, the table where food is laid out, and it suits ships that must feed thousands each day.
Things on a cruise ship.Deck chair: A deck chair from the Titanic has sold at auction for tens of thousands of dollars, a reminder that sitting on deck is an old tradition.
Things on a cruise ship.Swimming pool: The biggest cruise ships have several pools, plus water slides and surf simulators, all floating on salt water.
Things on a cruise ship.Lifeboat: After the Titanic's 1912 sinking, new rules required lifeboat space for everyone on board.
Things on a cruise ship.Cabin: Many cruise cabins are called staterooms, a term from old river steamboats whose rooms were named after states.
Things on a cruise ship.Captain: The idea that a captain can marry couples at sea is mostly a myth: it depends on the ship's flag-state laws.
Things on a cruise ship.Casino: Ship casinos open only once at sea beyond territorial waters, because they escape local gambling rules.
Things on a cruise ship.Theater: Big ships stage full Broadway-style musicals on board, often with performers rehearsing at sea.
Things on a cruise ship.Gangway: Shouting 'Gangway!' meaning 'clear the way' began aboard ships, where the gangway is the narrow walkway used to board.
Things on a cruise ship.Porthole: Portholes are round because square corners concentrate stress in glass and hull plates, and a circle spreads pressure evenly.
Things on a cruise ship.Balcony: Balcony cabins are so popular that modern cruise ships are designed around them, with hundreds of private verandas.
Things on a cruise ship.Muster station: Passengers must now attend a muster drill before the ship sails, a rule that came after the Costa Concordia disaster in 2012.
Things on a cruise ship.Shuffleboard: Shuffleboard descends from the English game 'shove-groat' of the 15th century, once played with coins on tables.
Things on a cruise ship.Runway: Runways belong to airports. Cruise ships have no need for them, though aircraft carriers have a flight deck.
Things on a cruise ship.Snowplow: A snowplow is for clearing roads, and no cruise ship needs one, though icebreakers exist.
Things on a cruise ship.Paddock: A paddock is a field for horses, so it belongs on a farm or racecourse, not on a ship.
Things on a cruise ship.Haystack: A haystack is a farm pile of hay, famous for the needle people lose in it, but not on a ship.
Things on a cruise ship.Pit lane: The pit lane is where racing teams service cars, so it isn't on a ship.
Things on a cruise ship.Cattle grid: A cattle grid is a metal grate set in a road to stop livestock crossing, so ships don't need one.
Things on a cruise ship.Tractor: A tractor tills fields, and it has no use on a ship.
Things on a cruise ship.Oil derrick: An oil derrick drills for oil, and it belongs to oil fields or offshore rigs, not cruise liners.
Things on a cruise ship.Fire hydrant: Fire hydrants are street water-supply points, and ships instead have internal fire mains and hoses.
Things on a cruise ship.Parking meter: The first parking meter appeared in Oklahoma City in 1935, and ships have no curbs, so no meters.
Things on a cruise ship.Toll booth: A toll booth collects road fees, but ships use ports with harbor fees instead.

Motorcycle makers.Harley-Davidson: Harley-Davidson was founded in 1903 in Milwaukee, and the first bikes were built in a small wooden shed.
Motorcycle makers.Ducati: Ducati is Italian, and its bikes use a "desmodromic" valve system, which uses an unusual mechanical way to close the valves.
Motorcycle makers.Yamaha: Yamaha began as a piano and organ maker in 1887, which is why its logo is three tuning forks.
Motorcycle makers.Kawasaki: Kawasaki also builds trains and ships through its heavy industries parent, and Kawasaki's famous green is its racing colour.
Motorcycle makers.Triumph: Triumph was founded in England by a German immigrant, Siegfried Bettmann, in the 1880s.
Motorcycle makers.Indian: Indian, founded in 1901, is America's oldest motorcycle brand, and its Scout was famous for a long time.
Motorcycle makers.Suzuki: Suzuki began making looms in 1909, and its Hayabusa was once the world's fastest production motorcycle.
Motorcycle makers.Honda: Honda is the world's biggest motorcycle maker, and the Super Cub has sold over 100 million units.
Motorcycle makers.BMW: BMW built its first motorcycle in 1923, and its flat-twin "boxer" engine is still used today.
Motorcycle makers.KTM: KTM is Austrian, and its bikes are known for their bright orange paint.
Motorcycle makers.Aprilia: Aprilia, founded near Venice, began by making bicycles after the war, and later won many world titles.
Motorcycle makers.Royal Enfield: Royal Enfield, founded in 1901, is often called the oldest motorcycle brand still in production, and now builds in India.
Motorcycle makers.Moto Guzzi: Moto Guzzi, from Mandello del Lario on Lake Como, uses an eagle in its logo and has built bikes since 1921.
Motorcycle makers.Norton: Norton, a British brand, has a long history of racing success at the Isle of Man TT.
Motorcycle makers.Ferrari: Ferrari makes only cars, and it sponsors racing teams, but it doesn't build production motorcycles.
Motorcycle makers.Lamborghini: Lamborghini started out making tractors, and now sticks to cars, though its sister brand Ducati makes bikes.
Motorcycle makers.Porsche: Porsche makes cars, and also built tractors in the 1950s, but never made motorcycles.
Motorcycle makers.Tesla: Tesla makes electric cars, trucks and batteries, but not motorcycles.
Motorcycle makers.Jaguar: Jaguar began as a sidecar maker in 1922 but now makes only cars.
Motorcycle makers.Volvo: Volvo builds cars, trucks and buses, but no motorcycles.
Motorcycle makers.Lexus: Lexus is Toyota's luxury car brand, and it doesn't build bikes.
Motorcycle makers.Bentley: Bentley makes luxury cars, and has never built motorcycles.
Motorcycle makers.Maserati: Maserati's trident logo comes from a fountain in Bologna, and it makes cars.
Motorcycle makers.Rolls-Royce: Rolls-Royce makes cars, and aircraft engines under a different company, but no motorcycles.

Things you'd find in a back garden.Gazebo: Gazebo is a possible mock-Latin joke word of the 1700s, meaning 'I shall gaze', for a little pavilion with a view.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Pergola: A pergola is a frame of posts and beams that supports climbing plants, and the word comes from Italian.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Shed: Sheds are the classic English hideaway, and a British 'Shed of the Year' contest is held each year.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Greenhouse: Greenhouses trap heat from sunlight, the same effect that gives the greenhouse gas its name.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Treehouse: Treehouses go back to at least Roman times, and Emperor Caligula reportedly had a banquet in one.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Arbor: An arbor is a shaded garden shelter, and the word is Latin for tree, as in Ann Arbor.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Trellis: A trellis is a lattice for climbing plants such as roses and clematis, and the name comes from the Latin for triple-woven.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Summerhouse: A summerhouse is a small garden building for warm days, once a place to take tea in Victorian gardens.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Pond: A new garden pond can attract frogs and dragonflies within a year, even if nobody stocks it.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Bird bath: A bird bath helps birds keep feathers clean, and shallow ones, a couple of centimeters deep, work best.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Birdhouse: Birdhouses work best if the hole size fits the species, and a hole that's too big invites starlings.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Chandelier: A chandelier hangs from an indoor ceiling, so it is a living-room fixture, not a garden one.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Mantelpiece: A mantelpiece is the shelf above an indoor fireplace, so it stays inside.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Banister: A banister is the handrail on a staircase indoors, and the word may come from 'baluster'.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Skirting board: A skirting board covers where a wall meets the floor inside, and is called a baseboard in the US.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Wardrobe: A wardrobe stores clothes indoors, and C. S. Lewis made one the door to Narnia.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Wallpaper: Wallpaper coats indoor walls, and Victorian wallpapers sometimes contained poisonous arsenic pigments.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Kitchen island: A kitchen island is a freestanding work surface indoors.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Sofa: A sofa belongs in the living room, and its name comes from the Arabic suffah, a bench.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Bathtub: Bathtubs go in bathrooms, though some gardens use old ones as ponds or planters.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Ceiling fan: A ceiling fan is an indoor item, since a garden has no ceiling.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Bunk bed: A bunk bed is a bedroom piece, and a garden has no ceiling for the top bunk.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Dishwasher: A dishwasher belongs in a kitchen, and was invented by Josephine Cochrane in 1886.
Things you'd find in a back garden.Bidet: A bidet is a bathroom fixture, and the name is French for a small horse, as one sits astride it.

Buildings where things are made.Factory: The word comes from Latin for 'make', and the first modern factory system took off in Britain's textile mills in the 1700s.
Buildings where things are made.Mill: Mills were among the first machines to harness water and wind power; some medieval watermills were in continuous use for centuries.
Buildings where things are made.Brewery: Beer is one of the oldest drinks; ancient Sumerians brewed it and even had a hymn to Ninkasi, the goddess of beer.
Buildings where things are made.Bakery: Bakeries are among the earliest food businesses, and in ancient Rome, baking guilds were regulated by the state.
Buildings where things are made.Foundry: Metal is melted and poured into molds here; bronze statues are still cast with the lost-wax method developed thousands of years ago.
Buildings where things are made.Workshop: A workshop is a small-scale place for crafting; the word has also come to mean a hands-on training session.
Buildings where things are made.Forge: A blacksmith heats iron to roughly 1,000 degrees Celsius in a forge until it glows orange and can be hammered into shape.
Buildings where things are made.Refinery: A refinery splits crude oil into petrol, diesel, jet fuel and more, using heat in tall distillation towers.
Buildings where things are made.Winery: Grapes are crushed and fermented here; the word is a signal that wine is produced on site rather than just sold.
Buildings where things are made.Distillery: Distilleries make spirits like whisky; Scotch must be aged in oak for at least three years to be sold under that name.
Buildings where things are made.Shipyard: Shipyards build and repair ships, and some of the largest cranes ever made are used in them to lift whole ship sections.
Buildings where things are made.Smithy: A smithy is where a blacksmith works, and the surname Smith is among the most common in English for that reason.
Buildings where things are made.Mint: Coins and banknotes are made at a mint; the word comes from the temple of Juno Moneta in ancient Rome, where coins were struck.
Buildings where things are made.Warehouse: A trap: goods are stored here but not made. Amazon-style fulfillment centers are huge warehouses, yet nothing is manufactured there.
Buildings where things are made.Museum: A museum preserves and displays objects, rather than manufacturing them. Britain's British Museum opened in 1759.
Buildings where things are made.Library: Libraries lend books, not produce them; the Library of Alexandria in ancient Egypt was one of the greatest ancient collections.
Buildings where things are made.Gallery: Art is displayed in a gallery, but it is made in a studio, so a gallery fails the 'made here' test.
Buildings where things are made.Hotel: A hotel provides rooms for guests. Nothing is manufactured there, though the Ritz made the word synonymous with luxury.
Buildings where things are made.Prison: Prisoners may work in some, but a prison's purpose is confinement, not production, so it is a trap.
Buildings where things are made.Showroom: A showroom displays cars or furniture for sale, while the products are made elsewhere, in a factory.
Buildings where things are made.Depot: A depot stores vehicles or goods, as with a bus depot; production happens elsewhere.
Buildings where things are made.Silo: A silo stores grain or other bulk materials, and some older ones also hold missiles. It does not manufacture anything.
Buildings where things are made.Archive: Archives keep records and documents safely; they preserve history rather than make products.
Buildings where things are made.Bank: A bank holds money and does not produce it. Banknotes are printed at a mint or a printing works, a different building.

Black tie attire.Tuxedo: Named after Tuxedo Park, New York, where it caught on in the 1880s, this is the American name for the dinner suit.
Black tie attire.Dinner jacket: The British name for the tuxedo came first: in the 1800s men wore it for dinners where a full tailcoat felt too stiff.
Black tie attire.Bow tie: A true black tie wears a self-tied one, and a pre-tied clip version is frowned upon by traditionalists.
Black tie attire.Cummerbund: Originally from India, it is a pleated waist sash worn with the pleats facing up, which were once used to hold a theatre ticket.
Black tie attire.Cufflinks: Dressy links with a decorative face, they replace buttons on French cuffs, and formal sets match the shirt studs.
Black tie attire.Dress shirt: For black tie it should be white with a pleated or piqué front and a turndown or wing collar, so no colours.
Black tie attire.Patent leather shoes: Patent leather's mirror-like lacquered shine has been a formal-shoe staple since the 1800s, when it was worn mostly for balls and the opera.
Black tie attire.Pocket square: The folded square of white linen or silk is a small final flourish, usually with a straight fold for formal wear.
Black tie attire.Shirt studs: These small buttons replace the usual ones down the front of a formal shirt, and they are often matched with cufflinks.
Black tie attire.Evening gown: Floor-length gowns are the usual dress for black tie events, such as Oscars night where they are the norm.
Black tie attire.Hoodie: A hoodie is simply too casual, and the invitation's dress code would turn it away at the door.
Black tie attire.Flip-flops: Open-toed beachwear is out for black tie, where polished closed shoes are expected.
Black tie attire.Tank top: Tank tops show bare arms and are far too casual for a formal evening.
Black tie attire.Sweatpants: Sweatpants are comfy and thus clash with the crisp, tailored feel of black tie.
Black tie attire.Baseball cap: A baseball cap would be removed indoors in any formal event, and black tie is no exception.
Black tie attire.Crocs: These foam clogs are loved for comfort and have no place at a formal dinner.
Black tie attire.Cargo shorts: Cargo shorts are the opposite of tailored, and no dress code allows bare knees in black tie.
Black tie attire.Fanny pack: Fanny packs are for comfort and carrying things hands-free, and they ruin the clean line of formalwear.
Black tie attire.Onesie: A onesie is cosy loungewear, and the dress code definitely does not allow it.
Black tie attire.Tracksuit: Tracksuits are athletic wear, and black tie demands tailoring.
Black tie attire.Board shorts: Board shorts are surf gear, so they would be a startling choice for formal evenings.
Black tie attire.Tailcoat: This is the trap: a tailcoat belongs to white tie, the even more formal dress code above black tie.
Black tie attire.Hawaiian shirt: A loud Hawaiian shirt is a holiday staple and is the opposite of the sleek restraint black tie requires.
Black tie attire.Denim jacket: Denim is casual workwear, and a jacket in it clashes with formal wear however smart it looks.

Fourth of July traditions.Fireworks: Fireworks have lit the Fourth since 1777, when Philadelphia held the first anniversary celebration with an elaborate show.
Fourth of July traditions.Barbecue: Cookouts mark the day, with ribs, burgers and corn, and families often put the grill on early.
Fourth of July traditions.Sparklers: These hand-held fireworks burn at around 1,000 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt some metals, so they are not as gentle as they look.
Fourth of July traditions.Parade: Small-town parades with marching bands and floats have run for over a century, and some towns hold them each year.
Fourth of July traditions.American flag: The flag's 13 stripes represent the original colonies, and the stars grew from 13 to 50 as states joined.
Fourth of July traditions.Hot dogs: Americans eat about 150 million of them on the day, and Nathan's holds a Coney Island eating contest each year on the Fourth.
Fourth of July traditions.Uncle Sam: The figure is thought to come from Samuel Wilson, a meat packer from Troy, New York, who supplied the army in the War of 1812.
Fourth of July traditions.Picnic: Blankets and baskets in a park while waiting for dusk and the show make this the most relaxed tradition.
Fourth of July traditions.Red white and blue: The colours of the Stars and Stripes decorate everything, and the red, white and blue gives the day a clear look.
Fourth of July traditions.Turkey dinner: Turkey dinner belongs to Thanksgiving in November, and it is not a summer holiday dish.
Fourth of July traditions.Shamrock: The shamrock is Ireland's emblem and belongs to St Patrick's Day in March, not to July.
Fourth of July traditions.Egg hunt: Egg hunts belong to Easter, when children look for hidden eggs symbolising new life in spring.
Fourth of July traditions.Mistletoe: Mistletoe belongs to Christmas, and the tradition of kissing beneath it goes back centuries.
Fourth of July traditions.Menorah: The menorah holds the lights for Hanukkah, an eight-night Jewish winter festival.
Fourth of July traditions.Cupid: Cupid is Valentine's Day's figure, and is the Roman equivalent of the Greek god Eros.
Fourth of July traditions.Candy corn: Candy corn is a Halloween sweet created in the 1880s, and is out of place in July.
Fourth of July traditions.Jack-o'-lantern: Jack-o'-lanterns are carved pumpkins from Halloween, and their name comes from an Irish folk tale of Stingy Jack.
Fourth of July traditions.Christmas tree: The Christmas tree is a winter tradition popularised in Germany, and has no link to summer.
Fourth of July traditions.Maypole: The maypole dance belongs to spring's May Day, when people circle a pole with ribbons.
Fourth of July traditions.Mooncake: Mooncakes are eaten at the Mid-Autumn Festival in East Asia, and they are far from American summers.
Fourth of July traditions.Hot cross bun: Hot cross buns are traditionally eaten on Good Friday in Britain, and their crosses mark the occasion.
Fourth of July traditions.Stocking: Stockings are hung by the fireplace at Christmas, so they are a December item.
Fourth of July traditions.Dreidel: Dreidels are four-sided spinning tops used in a Hanukkah game, each side marked with a Hebrew letter.
Fourth of July traditions.Advent calendar: Advent calendars count down the days to Christmas with little windows to open, and so have no place in July.

Holidays known for giving gifts.Christmas: Gift-giving at Christmas echoes the Magi's gifts and St. Nicholas; Americans spend hundreds of billions of dollars each year on it.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Hanukkah: Hanukkah gifts are a modern tradition, partly shaped by Christmas; the older custom was giving small coins called gelt.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Valentine's Day: Valentine's Day gifts include cards, flowers and chocolate; the first commercial Valentine cards appeared in the early 1800s.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Diwali: At Diwali families exchange sweets and gifts, and many businesses give bonuses and dried fruit boxes to staff.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Eid al-Fitr: Eid al-Fitr ends Ramadan with new clothes, gifts and 'eidi' money, usually given to children.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Kwanzaa: Kwanzaa includes zawadi, handmade or educational gifts for children, given on the last day of the week-long holiday.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Chinese New Year: At Chinese New Year people give red envelopes with money to children, since red is considered lucky.
Holidays known for giving gifts.St. Nicholas Day: On St. Nicholas Day on December 6 children in much of Europe wake to sweets in their shoes, which inspired the Santa Claus legend.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Three Kings Day: On Three Kings Day, January 6, children in Spain and Latin America get gifts, brought by the Magi rather than Santa.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Mother's Day: Mother's Day cards and flowers are a huge business; the US holiday was started by Anna Jarvis, who later campaigned against its commercialism.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Memorial Day: Memorial Day honors fallen US soldiers, so it is observed with remembrance, not gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Labor Day: Labor Day celebrates workers with barbecues and a day off, and gifts aren't a custom.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Groundhog Day: Groundhog Day has a groundhog predicting winter's end; Punxsutawney Phil has seen his shadow in most years.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Earth Day: Earth Day, first held in 1970, focuses on environmental action and not gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Bastille Day: Bastille Day, July 14, marks the 1789 storming of the prison, with parades and fireworks, not gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Yom Kippur: Yom Kippur is the Jewish Day of Atonement, a solemn fast, not a gift-giving day.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Ash Wednesday: Ash Wednesday starts Lent with ashes on the forehead as a mark of penitence; it has no gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Good Friday: Good Friday remembers the crucifixion; it's a day of reflection, and gifts aren't customary.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Lent: Lent is a 40-day period of fasting and penance before Easter, rather than gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Guy Fawkes Night: Guy Fawkes Night, November 5, has bonfires and fireworks, recalling the 1605 Gunpowder Plot; no gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.April Fools' Day: April Fools' Day is for pranks rather than presents; its origins are unclear.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Fourth of July: Fourth of July celebrates American independence with fireworks and barbecues, not gifts.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Flag Day: Flag Day, June 14, honors the US flag, adopted in 1777, and isn't a gift occasion.
Holidays known for giving gifts.Arbor Day: Arbor Day encourages planting trees; it started in Nebraska in 1872 and isn't about gifts.

Actual Nobel Prize winners.Marie Curie: The only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911; her notebooks are still radioactive.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Albert Einstein: He won the 1921 Physics Nobel for the photoelectric effect, not for relativity, which the committee considered too controversial.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Malala Yousafzai: She became the youngest Nobel laureate ever, receiving the Peace Prize in 2014 at age 17 for her campaign for girls' education.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Dalai Lama: Tenzin Gyatso received the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize for his nonviolent struggle for Tibet's freedom.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Ernest Hemingway: He won the 1954 Nobel in Literature, partly for The Old Man and the Sea, but was too injured from two plane crashes to travel to Stockholm.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Toni Morrison: Author of Beloved, she won the 1993 Literature prize and was the first Black woman to win a Nobel in that category.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Bob Dylan: The 2016 Literature Nobel went to the songwriter, the first musician to win it; he took weeks to even acknowledge it.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Mother Teresa: She won the 1979 Peace Prize for her work with the poor in Calcutta, and was made a saint in 2016.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Nelson Mandela: He shared the 1993 Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk for ending apartheid peacefully, and became South Africa's president the next year.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Barack Obama: He won the Peace Prize in 2009, only nine months into his presidency, which surprised many, including himself.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Niels Bohr: The Danish physicist won the 1922 Physics prize for his atomic model, and his son Aage also won one in 1975.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Alexander Fleming: He shared the 1945 Medicine Nobel for penicillin, which he discovered after noticing mould killed bacteria in a forgotten dish.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Winston Churchill: Britain's wartime prime minister won the 1953 Literature Nobel for his historical writing and oratory, not for his politics.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Stephen Hawking: Despite his fame for black hole radiation, he never won the Nobel Prize, since it could not be tested by observation.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Mahatma Gandhi: He was nominated several times for the Peace Prize but never won, and the committee later publicly expressed regret over it.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Mark Twain: The Huckleberry Finn author never won; the Literature prize began in 1901, and he died in 1910.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Carl Sagan: The Cosmos astronomer won a Pulitzer Prize for The Dragons of Eden, but never a Nobel.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Thomas Edison: Despite his inventions, Edison never won a Nobel, though a rumour once had him sharing one with Tesla in 1915; it wasn't true.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Nikola Tesla: He never received a Nobel Prize; a 1915 newspaper report that he and Edison would share one proved false.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Leo Tolstoy: The War and Peace author was nominated for the Nobel but never won, and he even asked not to receive it.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Franz Kafka: He died in 1924 largely unknown, and the Nobel never came for him, as his fame grew after death.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.James Joyce: Author of Ulysses never won the Nobel, despite being one of the 20th century's most influential novelists.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Virginia Woolf: The Mrs Dalloway author never won the Nobel, though she is a giant of modernism.
Actual Nobel Prize winners.Isaac Newton: He lived long before the prizes began in 1901, so the Nobel never had the chance.
